category_feedback.specific_evidence: expanded_walkthrough.title is 'When the child predicts the same number for any time span — repairing the time-doesn't-multiply trap at Grade 2' and rationale describes the trap concretely, but the walkthrough never cites or aligns with named research. recovery_moves are good ('Always show the formula: rule x time = prediction', 'Use repeated addition as a bridge', 'Practice with multiple time spans') but they don't BRANCH by what the diagnostic told you about the child — they're a single linear sequence.
category_feedback.required_fix: Cite a specific research anchor for the time-doesn't-multiply / rate misconception (e.g., Carpenter & Moser CGI 'multiplicative compare' or 'measurement-rate' problem types, or Thompson & Saldanha on rate reasoning) by name in the rationale. Then split recovery_moves into branches keyed to the diagnostic: (a) if the child re-states the rule unchanged, build skip-counting on the number line first; (b) if the child adds but loses count, give the explicit 'Day 1: ___, Day 2: ___, Total: ___' chart; (c) if the child multiplies one span correctly but freezes on a longer one, scaffold doubling (5 days = 25, so 10 days = 25 + 25).

category_feedback.specific_evidence: expanded_walkthrough.rationale frames the trap conceptually ('PREDICTION = RULE x TIME', 'rule per unit x number of units = prediction') and the lesson does let children invent rules at Station C and stretch with 2-rule predictions, but the misconception is not named in research-grounded terms. common_misconceptions list ('Time doesn't matter', 'Repeated addition is wrong', 'I just say the rule') reads as classroom-observed rather than research-anchored — no reference to Carpenter & Moser CGI problem types, Thompson & Saldanha on rate, or Lamon on proportional reasoning.
category_feedback.required_fix: In expanded_walkthrough.rationale, explicitly name the misconception in research terms — e.g., 'This is the rate-as-state confusion (Thompson & Saldanha, 2003): the child treats 5 buses/day as a static count rather than an iterable rate.' Add one sentence comparing strategies in step 4 of action — e.g., 'Some pairs will skip-count by 5s on the number line; others will write 5+5+5+5+5; a few will jump to 5x5. Lift up all three and name them as different paths to the same prediction so children see strategy choice as legitimate.'
